html:
The Tunxis were an Algonquian people of the Farmington River valley in central Connecticut. They were one of several small Native communities of the lower Connecticut valley, often counted among the Wappinger peoples, and are known mainly through their dealings with English settlers.

In 1634, soon after colonists from Massachusetts Bay moved into the valley, smallpox killed many of them. After the Pequot War of 1636 to 1638 they sold land to the English, and the town of Farmington grew up beside their village. Their neighbours included the Podunk, the Wangunk and the Quinnipiac.

In the 1700s many Tunxis became Christians. In the 1780s most of the remaining families left with other Native Christians of New England to found Brothertown in New York, led by the Mohegan preacher Samson Occom.
